payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Compared with the source, does the edited image retain a visibly photographic appearance in its subject matter?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited subject matter still reads as photographic rather than wholly drawn or cartoon-rendered; fail if it no longer reads as photographic; unknown if this cannot be judged from the images.
node.source_quote: Make this look like a comic book photo
node.endpoint: The subject matter remains visibly photographic while receiving the requested style.
node.necessity: The phrase requests a comic-book photo, not merely a comic-book drawing; losing the photographic appearance leaves the requested combined visual result incomplete.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image retains photographic-looking street details: cars, buildings, utility wires, and the pedestrian have natural textures, perspective, and lighting rather than wholly drawn or cartoon-rendered forms. Compared with the source, the scene remains recognizably photographic despite stronger contrast and stylization.

response.content: {"text":"The node checks only whether photographic appearance is retained, so it can pass even when the requested comic-book treatment is absent. The trace supports that narrow finding, but does not establish that the requested style was applied; the edited image appears largely photographic, with at most stronger contrast and stylization. Keep photographic retention as a required criterion, but make the decision assess the combined endpoint: whether the image has visibly acquired comic-book styling while still reading as a photo. Distinguish no progress from partial progress and completion, using concrete visual evidence for each; do not treat ordinary contrast changes as sufficient comic-book styling without evidence. The reference label is aggregate guidance, not proof that this individual criterion should fail. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported."}
